- If sentiment is consistently negative (≤0.33) over recent days, reduce forecast slope and avoid upward momentum; price may mean-revert or dip further.
- If forecast shows strong upward trend (e.g., >72.5) with sentiment neutral or positive, check for over-optimism — actuals often overshoot then correct, especially after spikes.
- When true outcome spikes sharply (e.g., >75) and forecast is flat or rising slowly, model underestimates volatility — adjust upward by 2–5% for next period if sentiment is bullish.
- If forecast is flat or slightly rising but true outcome drops sharply (e.g., <70), sentiment is bearish — model may be ignoring negative signals; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next period.
- If sentiment is mixed or neutral (0.33–0.67) and forecast is trending, check for lag — actuals often move 1–2 days ahead of forecast; adjust for 1–3 day lag in horizon.
- Avoid linear extrapolation — if recent 3–5 days show volatility, forecast should curve or adjust for mean reversion toward 65–75 range unless sentiment strongly bullish.
- If sentiment is bullish (≥0.67) and forecast is rising slowly, consider “overshoot correction” — actuals often peak then drop; reduce forecast slope by 10–20% after peak.
- If forecast is rising steadily but true outcome is flat or falling, sentiment may be misleading — reduce forecast by 1–2% per day if sentiment is weak or mixed.
- If sentiment is bearish and forecast is rising, model is ignoring sentiment — reduce forecast by 2–5% for next period.
- If forecast is rising sharply and sentiment is neutral or mixed, check for “false breakout” — actuals often correct within 3–5 days; cap forecast at 1–2% above recent high.
